## Observations

1. Because all sizes are positive, a valid top is strictly smaller than its bottom and therefore appears earlier in the sorted list. A top at index \(i\) fits on a bottom at index \(j\) exactly when \(2A_i \le A_j\).
2. For a fixed bottom, the eligible tops form a prefix of the list. The prefix may be empty, and each index in it counts separately, even when several mochi have the same size.
3. As the bottom moves from left to right, its size never decreases, so the eligible prefix can only stay the same or grow.
4. Each valid pair is counted under exactly one bottom. The total can exceed a signed 32-bit integer.

## Solution sketch

1. “Because all sizes are positive, a valid top is strictly smaller than its bottom and therefore appears earlier in the sorted list. A top at index \(i\) fits on a bottom at index \(j\) exactly when \(2A_i \le A_j\).” Read the list in its given order and visit every index as a possible bottom. Use the doubled-size comparison so that a top exactly half the bottom's size is included without any rounding.
2. “For a fixed bottom, the eligible tops form a prefix of the list. The prefix may be empty, and each index in it counts separately, even when several mochi have the same size.” Initialize a prefix length and a running total to zero. For each bottom, advance the prefix length while the next index is before the bottom and its mochi fits. Add the resulting prefix length to the total. An empty prefix contributes zero, and repeated sizes need no special handling.
3. “As the bottom moves from left to right, its size never decreases, so the eligible prefix can only stay the same or grow.” Keep the prefix length between bottoms rather than resetting it. The bottom scan and the prefix boundary each advance at most \(N\) times, so the algorithm takes \(O(N)\) time and \(O(1)\) auxiliary space beyond the stored \(O(N)\) input list.
4. “Each valid pair is counted under exactly one bottom. The total can exceed a signed 32-bit integer.” Print the running total after the scan. Python integers can hold the full count, and if no pair fits, the total remains zero.
